source.title_on_document: Design and evaluation of an AI-based application to enhance creativity in design thinking workshops

paper_design_summary: Economics and management undergraduates in two different classes completed an AI-assisted design-thinking workshop about a new space hotel business (Workshop A) or a human-only workshop about a new food business (Workshop B). The analyses retained 88 respondents (43 in A and 45 in B) and used their groups' brainstorming ideas and final selected ideas, measuring idea counts and externally rated novelty and usability. The authors acknowledge that differences in participants and themes could not be controlled because the workshops were held in different classes (PDF pp. 2, 4–5 and 10, Sections 2.1, 2.3 and 4; Tables 3 and 6).

studies.label: Comparison of AI-assisted and human-only design-thinking workshops

assignment.what_was_assigned: AI-assisted Workshop A and human-only Workshop B were implemented in different classes, with different business themes. The paper describes a comparison of these classes and does not report random allocation of people or classes.
assignment.quote: There is a limitation to this study: it is not possible to control for the effects of different themes or participants joining the workshops, which were difficult to avoid, given that we held two workshops in different classes.
assignment.locator: PDF p. 10 (printed p. 2170), Section 4, limitations paragraph; condition descriptions on PDF p. 2 (printed p. 2162), Section 2.1.

arms.name: Workshop A (WS-A; with AI)
arms.description: AI-assisted workshop on New Space Hotel Business in a different class from Workshop B. Table 3 reports 54 workshop participants, 43 extracted responses, 19 groups and 19 groups retained for idea evaluation (PDF p. 5, printed p. 2165).

arms.name: Workshop B (WS-B; human-only)
arms.description: Human-only workshop on New Food Business in a different class from Workshop A. Table 3 reports 104 workshop participants, 45 extracted responses, 25 groups and 15 groups retained for idea evaluation (PDF p. 5, printed p. 2165).

participants.exclusions: Responses lacking pre- or post-survey responses or either creativity item were excluded. Table 3 reports 54 workshop participants and 43 retained responses in Workshop A, and 104 workshop participants and 45 retained responses in Workshop B. Counts excluded by reason are not stated. (PDF p. 4, printed p. 2164, Section 2.3, final paragraph; PDF p. 5, printed p. 2165, Table 3.)
participants.who: Bachelor students majoring in economics and management in two different classes. The analyzed people count is the retained survey sample: 43 respondents in Workshop A and 45 in Workshop B; Table 6 explicitly labels the comparison N=88. Output evaluation used the groups to which retained respondents belonged, with 19 groups in A and 15 in B. Outcome-specific people counts for novelty and usability are not stated.
participants.quote: Both WS-A and WS-B were held in the class attended by the bachelor students majoring in economics and management.
participants.locator: PDF p. 4 (printed p. 2164), Section 2.3, final paragraph; PDF p. 5 (printed p. 2165), Table 3 and Table 6 heading.

ai_tool.name_model: Custom AI-based Application; Figure 2 labels the AI agent “Chat GPT4.0 LLM”.
ai_tool.how_used: Teams used a tablet interface. AI generated interview follow-up questions, alternative How Might We statements and up to six brainstorming ideas presented alongside human ideas; teams selected three ideas from the combined pool. PDF p. 3 (printed p. 2163), Section 2.2, Table 1 and Figure 2.

task.description: Design-thinking workshop using Discover, Define, Develop and Deliver phases: interviews, How Might We questions, brainstorming, then selection and presentation of three business ideas. Workshop A addressed New Space Hotel Business; Workshop B addressed New Food Business. Workshops were conducted in Japanese (PDF pp. 2–3, printed pp. 2162–2163, Section 2.1 and Table 1).

outcomes.name: Number of ideas generated during brainstorming
outcomes.question: with_ai

contrasts.reported: Workshop A (with AI): M=11.05, SD=4.705; Workshop B (human-only): M=15.40, SD=8.606; t(86)=−2.925, p=.004, Cohen’s d=.63 (as printed). Table 6 is labeled N=88. Ideas were counted from brainstorming post-its. The paper describes group outputs but reports these tests in a participant-count table; the mapping from group outputs to participant observations is not explained. Section 3.2 agrees with Table 6 that Workshop B generated more ideas; Section 4 contains a conflicting sentence saying the quantity was lower in only-human teams.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 2165), Table 6, No. of ideas row and Section 3.2; measurement on PDF p. 4 (printed p. 2164), Section 2.3; conflicting sentence on PDF p. 9 (printed p. 2169), Section 4.

contrasts.reported: Workshop A (with AI): M=2.9721, SD=.42619; Workshop B (human-only): M=3.1783, SD=.37508; t(84)=−2.382, p=.019, Cohen’s d=.52 (as printed). Scores average each team’s three selected ideas, rated on a 5-point scale by five external evaluators: two senior designers, a professional engineer and two bachelor’s students. Table 6 is labeled N=88, but this row reports df=84 and does not give outcome-specific arm counts. The outputs are group-level; the mapping to observations in the participant-count analysis is not explained.

The acknowledgement states that the company will use the research results to develop the AI-based Application. Coauthors Kazuko Katayama and Ryota Nishioka are affiliated with Smart Process Co., Ltd.
company_involvement.locator: PDF p. 10 (printed p. 2170), Acknowledgement; PDF p. 1 (printed p. 2161), author affiliations.

eligibility.reason: This is a comparison of workshops implemented in different classes, with different participants and different topics, rather than a reported random assignment of people to AI assistance. The authors explicitly acknowledge the different-class design and inability to control participant and theme differences (PDF p. 10, printed p. 2170, Section 4; condition descriptions on PDF p. 2, Section 2.1). The analyzed sample is 88 people, with 43 retained responses in A and 45 in B (PDF p. 5, Table 3 and Table 6 heading), and novelty and usability are external ratings of the groups’ produced ideas (PDF p. 4, Section 2.3 and Table 2). Criteria 2 and 3 are met, but the class-based non-random comparison fails criterion 1 and is observational context.

one_line_finding: In a non-random comparison of different classes (N=88), the AI workshop had fewer ideas (11.05 vs 15.40, p=.004), lower novelty (2.9721 vs 3.1783, p=.019) and higher usability (3.6946 vs 3.1348, p<.001) than the human-only workshop (PDF p. 5, printed p. 2165, Table 6).
